title: Concrete-hash security for restricted numerical circuit families
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: Identify a checkable family of quantized inference circuits for which concrete-hash Fiat–Shamir GKR is adaptively sound. Target circuits with size \(S\le10^{12}\), depth \(D\le10^4\), and an explicit 128-bit security analysis that states which compiler rewrites preserve the guarantee.
status: Khovratovich, Rothblum and Soukhanov’s 2025 attack covers selected GKR circuits, including functionally equivalent rewrites. It does not establish that every fixed AI circuit is insecure.
why: Security can depend on the circuit’s implementation, so mathematical equivalence alone is insufficient.
key_works: Dmitry Khovratovich, Ron D. Rothblum, Lev Soukhanov (2025), [*How to Prove False Statements: Practical Attacks on Fiat-Shamir*, ePrint 2025/118](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/118).

title: Work overhead required for white-box-resistant Fiat–Shamir
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: Determine the minimum additional prover work required for XFS-style resistance to diagonalization. Target at most 5% additional proving and verification work under the stated relativized-oracle model, and determine whether comparable protection can avoid proof-of-work.
status: Arnon and Yogev’s XFS construction, published at CRYPTO 2025, provides security evidence in a relativized random-oracle model. That result does not establish security for arbitrary concrete hashes.
why: A defensive transform must remain affordable when applied to every inference or training receipt.
key_works: Gal Arnon, Eylon Yogev (2025), [*Towards a White-Box Secure Fiat-Shamir Transformation*, ePrint 2025/329](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/329).

title: Quantum security loss for unmodified tensor sumcheck transcripts
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: For ordinary Fiat–Shamir applied to \(m\)-round, degree-\(d\) tensor sumcheck, prove a QROM security loss of \(O(q^2\operatorname{poly}(m,d))\), or establish a protocol-specific obstruction. Cover \(m\le64\), \(d\le8\), and quantum hash-query budget \(q\), without substituting a different transform.
status: General multi-round reductions can incur substantial round-dependent losses. Improved modified transforms exist, leaving the precise frontier for the unchanged tensor protocol as the target.
why: A quantum-resistant commitment primitive does not automatically confer a complete quantum soundness bound.
key_works: Jelle Don, Serge Fehr, Christian Majenz (2020), [*The Measure-and-Reprogram Technique 2.0: Multi-Round Fiat-Shamir and More*, arXiv:2003.05207](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.05207); Thomas Attema et al. (2026), [*The Fiat–Shamir Transformation of \((\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_\mu)\)-Special-Sound Interactive Proofs*](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00145-025-09569-y).

title: Practical straight-line extraction transforms for numerical PIOPs
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: Specialize straight-line-extractable transforms to 32–64-round tensor PIOPs, including all transcript and recomputation costs. Target at most 2× prover work and 1.25× proof bytes relative to ordinary Fiat–Shamir, with explicit polynomial extraction time.
status: Rotem and Tessaro already give multi-round transforms, including a QROM-secure variant. The open target concerns concrete numerical-proof overhead, rather than existence of such transforms.
why: Efficient extraction can simplify recursive security arguments without making proving prohibitively expensive.
key_works: Lior Rotem, Stefano Tessaro (2025; preprint 2024), [*Straight-Line Knowledge Extraction for Multi-Round Protocols*, ePrint 2024/1724](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1724).

title: Algebraic cryptanalysis of fully bound numerical transcripts
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: Publish a reproducible attack frontier coupling Poseidon/Poseidon2 challenge generation with actual sumcheck and low-degree verification equations. Cover at least 100 field/width/round configurations, including deployed full-round configurations, and distinguish challenge bias from acceptance of a false statement.
status: The 2026 Poseidon-based Fiat–Shamir study reports no meaningful forgeries, even with heavily reduced parameters. Its negative experiments leave substantial room for broader, independently replicated analysis.
why: Algebraic hashes and algebraic verifier equations may interact differently from isolated hash benchmarks.
key_works: Hayk Hovhannisyan, Nerses Asaturyan, Gohar Hovhannisyan (2026), [*Cryptanalysis of Poseidon-Based Fiat-Shamir Protocols*, ePrint 2026/409](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/409).

title: Optimal challenge independence for shared polynomial proof graphs
subfield: Fiat–Shamir and concrete-hash foundations
open: Characterize which dependency graphs permit polynomial checks to share random challenges safely. Target \(2^{20}\) degree-at-most-8 checks, \(O(\lambda+\log M)\) random bits per independent stage, and total error at most \(2^{-128}\), or prove a larger randomness requirement.
status: GAPP supplies algebraic packing and aggregation machinery. Optimal randomness use across dependent numerical checks is a further question.
why: Legal challenge reuse controls both batching efficiency and the soundness of tensor-proof composition.
key_works: Chaya Ganesh, Sikhar Patranabis, Shubh Prakash, Nitin Singh (2026; preprint 2024), [*GAPP: Generic Aggregation of Polynomial Protocols*, ePrint 2024/1685](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1685).

title: QROM extraction for coordinate-wise lattice commitments
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Extend Akita’s coordinate-wise, many-round extraction analysis to quantum hash queries while preserving its implemented folding and batching schedule. Target a justified knowledge-error bound at most \(2^{-128}\) for \(q\le2^{64}\), with every reduction loss included.
status: Akita’s September 2026 analysis is in the classical ROM; its Section 14 explicitly leaves QROM analysis open.
why: Estimated lattice hardness and quantum security of the complete proof transcript are separate guarantees.
key_works: Quang Dao et al. (2026), [*Akita: A High-Performance Lattice-Based Polynomial Commitment Scheme*, Section 14](https://assets.layerzero.network/pdf/akita.pdf); Valerio Cini et al. (2024), [*Polynomial Commitments from Lattices: Post-Quantum Security, Fast Verification and Transparent Setup*, ePrint 2024/281](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/281).

title: Rigorous response-norm tails for optimized lattice folding
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Prove the response-distribution assumptions behind optimized later-fold schedules, or replace them with rigorous bounds and quantify the cost. Target honest-prover rejection probability at most \(2^{-40}\) across \(10^6\) folds, within 20% of the heuristic schedule’s proof size and proving time.
status: Akita explicitly identifies its optimized response-model premise as heuristic and requests either a proof or a quantified replacement.
why: Rare norm failures can undermine long-running proof-service reliability even when soundness remains intact.
key_works: Quang Dao et al. (2026), [*Akita*, Section 14 and Appendix G](https://assets.layerzero.network/pdf/akita.pdf).

title: Hiding lattice commitments without destroying sparse-input savings
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Construct a zero-knowledge sparse lattice PCS whose commitment work is \(O(s\operatorname{polylog}N)\) for \(s\) nonzero entries. At density at most \(1/256\), target no more than 20% additional proof bytes and 2× prover work, with simulation for batched openings and explicit leakage.
status: Akita lists native zero knowledge as future work. Its sparse-commitment performance should not be treated as an existing hiding guarantee.
why: Dense masking can erase the sparse one-hot advantage used by efficient lookup-heavy provers.
key_works: Quang Dao et al. (2026), [*Akita*, ePrint 2026/1983](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1983), [full paper](https://assets.layerzero.network/pdf/akita.pdf).

title: Small-proof polylogarithmic verification for lattice commitments
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Combine transparent setup, polylogarithmic verification and proof size, and quasilinear proving with openings at most 16 KiB and verification within 5 ms on one M4 Max CPU core at \(N=2^{30}\). Require a justified 128-bit target from standard Module-SIS, counting setup, norm growth, and security-dependent dimensions.
status: Polylogarithmic lattice verification already exists. Akita offers constant-root verification and reports 61–72 kB proofs in its benchmark regimes; the joint asymptotic and concrete target above is not established by these results.
why: Large tensor proofs need small communication and fast verification simultaneously.
key_works: Valerio Cini et al. (2024), [*Polynomial Commitments from Lattices*, ePrint 2024/281](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/281); Quang Dao et al. (2026), [*Akita*, ePrint 2026/1983](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1983).

title: The joint constant-proof and linear-work multilinear PCS frontier
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Obtain a pairing-based multilinear PCS with at most \(2G_1+3\mathbb F\) opening elements, a two-term pairing check, \(O(N)\) field work, and at most \(N+o(N)\) MSM scalars. Demonstrate the joint target at \(N\ge2^{20}\), counting auxiliary commitments and setup.
status: Vela reports a 200-byte opening but uses \(O(N\log N)\) field work; Carina uses \(O(N)\) field work with a 452-byte opening. Neither supplies the requested combination.
why: Minimizing proof bytes alone can increase the dominant prover cost.
key_works: Yuncong Zhang (2026), [*Vela and Carina: Fast Pairing-Based Multilinear Polynomial Commitments from Reciprocal Polynomials*, ePrint 2026/1438](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1438).

title: Fast pairing PCS knowledge soundness outside the algebraic group model
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Prove knowledge soundness of reciprocal-polynomial multilinear commitments against non-algebraic adversaries in the ROM under a stated falsifiable assumption, or identify a separation. Target justified total error at most \(2^{-128}\) for \(N=2^{30}\), preserving the commitment and opening algorithms.
status: Vela/Carina uses AGM+ROM. Lipmaa’s 2025 Plonk result removes AGM in a different setting, making this a scheme-specific extension.
why: Extractability assumptions propagate into claims about knowledge of hidden weights and witnesses.
key_works: Yuncong Zhang (2026), [*Vela and Carina*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1438); Helger Lipmaa (2025), [*Plonk is Simulation Extractable in ROM Under Falsifiable Assumptions*, ePrint 2025/1759](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1759).

title: PCS verifier lower bounds with reusable cryptographic preprocessing
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Extend communication-core lower bounds to Bulletproofs-style discrete-log IPA commitments with transparent generators, no verifier trapdoor, and \(S\) bits of reusable preprocessing. Determine an online verification tradeoff such as \(V=\Omega(N/S)\) for explicitly defined models, including \(S=N^\alpha\) with \(\alpha\in\{0,1/4,1/2\}\).
status: Bhadauria et al. give communication-core bounds of \(\Omega(\sqrt N)\), \(\Omega(N)\), and \(\Omega(\log N)\) for Hyrax, Bulletproofs, and Dory respectively. These are not unconditional bounds for every PCS.
why: Repeated model use changes what a verifier can afford to precompute.
key_works: Rishabh Bhadauria, Alexander R. Block, Prantar Ghosh, Justin Thaler (2025), [*SNARK Lower Bounds via Communication Complexity*, ePrint 2025/1698](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1698).

title: Multipoint multilinear opening complexity after one commitment
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Determine optimal total work for \(k\) adversarially chosen multilinear evaluations following one \(O(N)\)-cost commitment. Target \(O(N+k\operatorname{polylog}N)\) total work for \(k\le\sqrt N\), with polylogarithmic proof size, or establish a matching lower bound.
status: Samaritan reports \(O(N+k\sqrt N)\) cryptographic work in its batched regime. That leaves the stronger amortization target unresolved.
why: Many operator checks open the same weight or activation polynomial at different points.
key_works: Chaya Ganesh, Sikhar Patranabis, Nitin Singh (2025), [*Samaritan: Linear-time Prover SNARK from New Multilinear Polynomial Commitments*, ePrint 2025/419](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/419).

title: Public-parameter lower bounds for bivariate Lagrange commitments
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Determine whether \(O(m+n)\) public parameters are optimal for algebraic pairing commitments to arbitrary bidegree-\((m,n)\) polynomials. Seek either \(o(m+n)\) setup with \(O(mn)\) commitment and \(O(m+n)\) opening work, or a lower bound counting all preprocessing advice.
status: GAPP’s bivariate Lagrange-basis commitment achieves \(O(m+n)\) public parameters and opening cryptographic operations. Optimality or strict improvement is the proposed gap.
why: Large reusable setup data can undermine otherwise compact proof aggregation.
key_works: Chaya Ganesh et al. (2026), [*GAPP: Generic Aggregation of Polynomial Protocols*, ePrint 2024/1685](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1685).

title: Controlled malleability for richer tensor commitment transformations
subfield: Polynomial commitments and controlled algebraic operations
open: Characterize safe public transformations supporting permutations, reshapes, slices, and rank-\(r\) maps for \(r\le64\), with \(O(r\operatorname{polylog}N)\) additional verifier work. Require succinct transformation descriptions or preprocessed descriptor commitments, account for descriptor access, and reject transformations outside the declared family.
status: Faonio and Russo show that controlled linear malleability can support non-malleable sumcheck SNARKs even when the underlying PCS lacks simulation extractability. Richer tensor transformations require further analysis.
why: Tensor systems intentionally transform commitments, so permitted algebra must be distinguished from proof substitution.
key_works: Antonio Faonio, Luigi Russo (2026), [*Sumcheck-based zkSNARKs are Non-Malleable*, ePrint 2026/335](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/335).

title: Polynomial-depth IVC security in the ordinary ROM
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Prove knowledge soundness for polynomial-depth, two-curve numerical IVC in the ordinary ROM without an open-and-sign oracle or adversary algebraic representations. Target extraction polynomial in total trace length and inverse acceptance probability, including \(10^6\) proof steps.
status: Maller, Mohnblatt and Zapico prove polynomial-depth security in osROM, an explicitly stronger idealization. Transferring the guarantee is the remaining question.
why: Long execution certificates need a justified extraction theorem across the whole recursion.
key_works: Mary Maller, Nicolas Mohnblatt, Arantxa Zapico (2025), [*IVC in the Open-and-sign Random Oracle Model*, ePrint 2025/1663](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1663).

title: Recursive simulation extractability across evolving setup histories
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Combine PCD simulation extractability with adversarially updated, correlated SRS histories, including merging branches produced under different reachable setups. Target \(10^4\) updates and a \(10^6\)-node DAG with one explicit simulator/extractor analysis and total failure at most \(2^{-128}\).
status: PCD-specific simulation extractability and stronger updatable-SE definitions now have positive results. Their joint adaptive-recursion setting is the proposed extension.
why: Long-lived model histories can cross setup updates and organizational boundaries.
key_works: Behzad Abdolmaleki et al. (2026; preprint 2025), [*On the Simulation-Extractability of Proof-Carrying Data*, ePrint 2025/2037](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2037); Hamidreza Khoshakhlagh (2026), [*Revisiting Simulation Extractability in the Updatable Setting*, ePrint 2025/2117](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/2117).

title: Trapdoorless zero knowledge for standalone linearization gadgets
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Construct locally simulatable replacements for linearization-style commit-and-prove gadgets, or prove a minimum overhead. Target at most two additional commitments and 10% additional prover arithmetic, with security composing with sumcheck and lookup relations.
status: Lipmaa proves whole-protocol Plonk simulation extractability while showing that several standalone gadgets lack trapdoorless ZK. Global security therefore does not automatically supply the desired local contract.
why: Modular proof libraries need security interfaces matching how their components are reused.
key_works: Helger Lipmaa (2025), [*Plonk is Simulation Extractable in ROM Under Falsifiable Assumptions*, ePrint 2025/1759](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/1759).

title: Efficient adaptive-corruption simulation of streaming proof state
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Make proof-maintenance memory simulatable under \(10^6\) adaptively selected snapshots, conditional on explicitly exposed application state and outputs. Target at most 2× prover time and \(O(S+\operatorname{polylog}T)\) live storage, with a precise erasure and corruption model.
status: Afshar and Goyal introduce verifiable streaming computation and step-by-step ZK, including internal-state simulation. The concrete numerical, multiple-snapshot target extends that foundation.
why: Final-transcript ZK does not describe what an attacker learns from a live proof worker.
key_works: Abtin Afshar, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Verifiable Streaming Computation and Step-by-Step Zero-Knowledge*, ePrint 2025/251](https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/251).

title: Private stateless handoff of recursive numerical proofs
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Transfer a recursive proving task between independent workers while exposing only declared public state. Target polylogarithmic handoff bytes and persistent proof state, excluding the next worker’s fresh local witness, and at most 2× per-step cost on \(2^{24}\)-constraint steps.
status: Holography accumulation supplies stateless recursion for relevant SNARK classes. Private handoff with the stated concrete costs remains a further target.
why: Worker migration should not require disclosure of an entire private proof history.
key_works: Nikitas Paslis, Carla Ràfols, Alexandros Zacharakis (2026), [*Proof-Carrying Data via Holography Accumulation*, ePrint 2026/538](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/538).

title: From binding commitments to computationally unique witnesses
subfield: Recursive knowledge and adaptive simulation
open: Determine whether UP-style SNARK constructions extend to deterministic numerical executions whose hidden inputs are only computationally fixed by commitments. Seek proof and verification complexity polynomial in \(\lambda\) and \(\log T\), under falsifiable standard-model assumptions, or establish a barrier.
status: Mathialagan, Peters and Vaikuntanathan handle UP’s literal witness uniqueness in a reusable designated-verifier model. Computational binding does not make every committed-input relation information-theoretically unambiguous.
why: “Deterministic execution” and “unique NP witness” are different properties when inputs remain hidden.
key_works: Surya Mathialagan, Spencer Peters, Vinod Vaikuntanathan (2024), [*Adaptively Sound Zero-Knowledge SNARKs for UP*, ePrint 2024/227](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/227).

title: Tight epoch–query tradeoffs for reused numerical proof queries
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Specialize query-reuse bounds to matrix-product and lookup-trace encodings, retaining accept/reject leakage. Determine the epoch–query tradeoff within a constant factor for \(r\in\{1,2,4,16,256\}\), \(N=2^{20}\) through \(2^{40}\), and error \(2^{-128}\).
status: *Query-Reusable Proof Systems* gives nearly tight general tradeoffs and limitations on unrestricted statistical reuse. Structured numerical languages may permit sharper special cases.
why: Reusing hidden verifier tests across many receipts creates an adaptive-feedback channel.
key_works: Yuval Ishai, Eyal Kushilevitz, Varun Narayanan, Rafail Ostrovsky, Akash Shah (2025), [*Query-Reusable Proof Systems*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91134-7_12).

title: Concrete computational query reuse for a fixed model verifier
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Implement a designated-verifier numerical proof system safely reusing hidden query positions across \(10^6\) adaptive proofs, including malformed ones. Target less than 1 MiB verifier state and 10 ms online verification at \(N=2^{20}\), with explicit computational assumptions.
status: Positive query-reuse constructions exist when soundness or ZK is computational. The proposed numerical service benchmarks are additional.
why: A customer can amortize verification setup only if feedback does not enable tailored later forgeries.
key_works: Yuval Ishai et al. (2025), [*Query-Reusable Proof Systems*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91134-7_12).

title: Worst-case refresh cost for private authenticated numerical RAM
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Build private authenticated RAM for \(2^{30}\) 64-bit words, with at most \(10^4\) application probes per request and \(2^{20}\) extra refresh operations on any request, including epoch boundaries. Target p99 refresh slowdown below 2× and simulation over \(10^6\) adaptive requests.
status: Ishai, Ostrovsky and Shah already support ZK RAM updates using black-box symmetric primitives. Concrete worst-case refresh and latency bounds remain the application target.
why: Amortized bounds can conceal unacceptable pauses in mutable embedding and optimizer stores.
key_works: Yuval Ishai, Rafail Ostrovsky, Akash Shah (2025), [*Zero-Knowledge RAM: Doubly Efficient and Black-Box*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-91134-7_13).

title: Access-pattern lower bounds for offline and limited-lookahead AI proving
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Establish the bandwidth–privacy frontier when a prover knows the next \(B\) accesses before revealing memory traffic. Separate \(B=1\), \(B=\log N\), and \(B=N^\alpha\), determining when sublogarithmic overhead is possible with polylogarithmic private client storage.
status: Online ORAM has logarithmic bandwidth lower bounds, including strengthened models hiding operation boundaries. Those results do not automatically cover an already recorded tensor trace.
why: Offline proving may escape online barriers, but that requires a different theorem.
key_works: Pavel Hubáček, Michal Koucký, Karel Král, Veronika Slívová (2019), [*Stronger Lower Bounds for Online ORAM*, arXiv:1903.03385](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.03385).

title: Standard-model succinct proofs for expressive hidden-model inference
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Construct adaptively sound, publicly verifiable SNARGs for an explicitly NP-hard family of quantized inference statements from falsifiable standard-model assumptions using a non-black-box reduction. Target proof and verification complexity polynomial in \(\lambda,\log T\), or establish a sharply scoped barrier.
status: Gentry–Wichs establishes a broad black-box-reduction barrier; positive restricted-language constructions do not resolve general expressive hidden-input inference.
why: This would improve foundational assumptions rather than only optimize existing proof architectures.
key_works: Craig Gentry, Daniel Wichs (2011), [*Separating Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments From All Falsifiable Assumptions*, ePrint 2010/610](https://eprint.iacr.org/2010/610); Surya Mathialagan et al. (2024), [*Adaptively Sound Zero-Knowledge SNARKs for UP*](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/227).

title: Succinctness boosting without full witness extraction
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Boost mildly succinct SNARGs lacking full knowledge soundness. A numerical specialization should compress \(m/\lambda+\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,n)\)-length proofs to \(\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,n,\log m)\) under an explicitly stated weak-extraction premise.
status: Cheng–Goyal explicitly leaves boosting without, or with very weak, extractability open.
why: Cheap validity checks may lack the extractors required by existing compression methods.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*, DOI:10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56).

title: Succinctness boosting from nonadaptive inner soundness
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Determine whether nonadaptively sound mildly succinct proofs can be boosted for precommitted numerical workloads. Target an aggregate of \(10^6\) statements fixed before setup with polylogarithmic dependence on total execution length, and characterize later adaptive-request limitations.
status: Removing adaptive soundness from the boosting premise is another explicit Cheng–Goyal question.
why: Scheduled training and evaluation campaigns may permit weaker starting assumptions.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56).

title: CRS compression using only collision-resistant hashing
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Remove efficient RAM delegation from the CRS-shortening step of succinctness boosting, using collision-resistant hashing in addition to the starting proof system. Target CRS size \(\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,n,\log T)\) for \(T\)-step numerical programs.
status: Cheng–Goyal explicitly asks whether RAM delegation can be eliminated or replaced by CRHFs.
why: Large setup data and stronger assumptions can dominate changing-model deployments.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56).

title: Additive-overhead complexity-preserving proof generation
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Achieve generic succinctness boosting with prover time \(T+\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,\log T)\) and space \(S+\operatorname{poly}(\lambda,\log T)\), rather than multiplicative overhead. Specify the RAM model and charge randomness generation, setup, and output writing explicitly.
status: Replacing fixed multiplicative overhead with fixed additive overhead is a published Cheng–Goyal open question.
why: It asks whether the asymptotic cost of certification can approach execution itself.
key_works: Jiaqi Cheng, Rishab Goyal (2025), [*Boosting SNARKs and Rate-1 Barrier in Arguments of Knowledge*](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2025.56).

title: Certificate-size barriers for universally quantified numerical claims
subfield: Private RAM, reusable verification, and succinctness barriers
open: Classify restricted neural safety claims admitting polynomial-size witnesses for ordinary NP SNARKs. Seek certificate bounds in circuit size \(S\), precision \(b\), and unstable-ReLU count \(k\), including whether \(2^{o(k)}\operatorname{poly}(S,b)\) certificates are possible under stated assumptions.
status: Alsmann, Lange and Sälzer establish complexity results for quantized verification formulations. These do not make every universal safety property cheaply certifiable.
why: Compressing a supplied certificate does not make finding a universal-property certificate easy.
key_works: Eric Alsmann, Martin Lange, Marco Sälzer (2026), [*The Complexity of Verifying Feedforward Neural Networks in Quantised Settings*, arXiv:2605.29537](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29537).

title: V-trace correction with authenticated behavior probabilities
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Bind actor, target-policy, value checkpoints, and terminal masks while proving V-trace’s distinct clipped ratios and products. For \(0\le\bar c\le\min(1,\bar\rho)\), \(\bar\rho\le10\), discount at most 0.99, bounded rewards/values, and behavior probabilities at least \(2^{-24}\), keep target error below \(10^{-4}\) over 1,000 steps with linear proving work.
status: IMPALA establishes V-trace; zkUCB supplies a narrower bandit-verification result. The combined numerical and cryptographic target remains a proposed extension.
why: Forged behavior probabilities can invalidate an otherwise correctly calculated off-policy update.
key_works: Lasse Espeholt et al. (2018), [*IMPALA*, arXiv:1802.01561](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.01561); Xikun Jiang et al. (2024), [*Privacy-Preserving UCB Decision Process Verification via zk-SNARKs*, arXiv:2404.12186](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12186).

title: Private prioritized-replay normalization and priority refresh
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Prove each replay draw against the committed buffer state and unpredictable randomness, including priority exponents, positive-priority or zero-total rules, normalized importance weights, and TD-error refreshes. Target \(10^7\) transitions with \(O(\log N)\) authenticated work per draw/update while hiding indices and priorities.
status: Prioritized Experience Replay specifies the sampling and correction algorithm. The stated private proof system is a further target.
why: Correct cumulative arithmetic alone does not prevent a provider from choosing favorable samples.
key_works: Tom Schaul, John Quan, Ioannis Antonoglou, David Silver (2016; preprint 2015), [*Prioritized Experience Replay*, arXiv:1511.05952](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.05952).

title: Replay capacity and update-to-data ratio certificates
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Certify admission, FIFO eviction, update counters, and permitted transition reuse against one ordered environment log. Target \(10^8\) insertions into a \(10^6\)-entry buffer with less than 5% extra proof cost, including concurrent inserts and samples.
status: Fedus et al. analyze replay capacity and replay ratio as consequential algorithmic controls. Their work does not supply these stateful ZK guarantees.
why: Authentic individual samples do not establish compliance with the claimed replay regime.
key_works: William Fedus et al. (2020), [*Revisiting Fundamentals of Experience Replay*, arXiv:2007.06700](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.06700).

title: Double-Q selection and target-network synchronization
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Prove that action selection uses the online Q-network and evaluation uses the prescribed target checkpoint, including argmax ties and every scheduled target copy. Cover \(10^6\) updates with less than 5% linkage overhead beyond the two network proofs.
status: Double DQN establishes the separate selection/evaluation roles. A matched stateful ZK implementation meeting this target was not established in the reviewed sources.
why: Substituting an online or stale target network silently changes the learning algorithm.
key_works: Hado van Hasselt, Arthur Guez, David Silver (2016; preprint 2015), [*Deep Reinforcement Learning with Double Q-learning*, arXiv:1509.06461](https://arxiv.org/abs/1509.06461).

title: Soft actor-critic entropy and temperature-update proofs
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Prove twin-critic targets, reparameterized actor sampling, tanh change-of-variables, target averaging, and automatic temperature updates as one SAC transition. Target \(10^5\) updates of 10M-parameter networks at less than 10× total runtime, including commitments.
status: SAC provides the maximum-entropy algorithm and temperature tuning. Generic training proofs offer ingredients, but not this complete measured workload.
why: Omitting entropy corrections or temperature state changes the objective being certified.
key_works: Tuomas Haarnoja et al. (2018), [*Soft Actor-Critic Algorithms and Applications*, arXiv:1812.05905](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.05905); Haochen Sun et al. (2023), [*zkDL*, arXiv:2307.16273](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16273).

title: Mass-preserving categorical Bellman projection proofs
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Certify C51 support clipping, neighboring-bin interpolation, terminal handling, and probability-mass conservation under declared rounding. Target \(10^6\) transitions with 51 atoms, at most \(10^{-6}\) \(L_1\) error per distribution, and linear work in atom count.
status: Distributional RL establishes the categorical Bellman update. Its finite-precision proof kernel remains the proposed deliverable.
why: Small probability-mass errors can accumulate through repeated distributional updates.
key_works: Marc G. Bellemare, Will Dabney, Rémi Munos (2017), [*A Distributional Perspective on Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:1707.06887](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06887).

title: Quantile-Huber Bellman losses without quadratic witnesses
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Prove the exact all-pairs quantile-Huber loss and declared subgradient without materializing \(K^2\) residuals. For \(K=1{,}024\) and batches of 4,096 transitions, target \(O(K\log K)\) auxiliary work and storage per transition, including sign and threshold ties.
status: Quantile-regression RL supplies the objective. Exploiting ordering and prefix statistics for a succinct private proof is the proposed algorithmic frontier.
why: A quadratic auxiliary witness can erase the benefit of compact distributional representations.
key_works: Will Dabney, Mark Rowland, Marc G. Bellemare, Rémi Munos (2018), [*Distributional Reinforcement Learning with Quantile Regression*, arXiv:1710.10044](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.10044).

title: Recurrent replay burn-in and actor–learner staleness
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Certify stored recurrent-state origins, learner checkpoint selection, burn-in exclusion from loss, and permitted actor version lag. Target 256 actors and \(10^6\) replayed sequences, charging only executed burn-in and learning steps rather than complete episode replays.
status: R2D2 studies recurrent-state staleness and representational drift. Its remedies do not themselves establish the proposed provenance certificate.
why: A valid recurrent computation can start from an unauthorized or stale hidden state.
key_works: Steven Kapturowski et al. (2019), [*Recurrent Experience Replay in Distributed Reinforcement Learning*](https://willdabney.com/publication/r2d2/).

title: Conservative offline-RL penalty and sampling-error certificates
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Prove CQL’s data-action and sampled log-partition terms under a declared normalized reference measure. After fixing Q and proposal densities, use fresh conditional samples and bounded-Q/domination assumptions to certify per-update 99% coverage for error at most 0.01; budget simultaneous adaptive coverage separately.
status: CQL supplies conservative-value theory and practical sampled objectives. A proof of sampled arithmetic alone does not establish its population lower-bound claims.
why: Numerical correctness and statistical validity must both hold for a meaningful conservative-value certificate.
key_works: Aviral Kumar, Aurick Zhou, George Tucker, Sergey Levine (2020), [*Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning*, arXiv:2006.04779](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.04779).

title: Implicit-Q expectiles and logged-action restriction proofs
subfield: Off-policy replay and distributional zkRL
open: Prove IQL expectile regression, target bootstrap, and clipped advantage-weighted cloning as one transition. Certify that every critic action query uses a committed logged action, targeting \(10^6\) transitions and a 100M-parameter policy below 10× total overhead.
status: IQL avoids querying Q on unseen actions and extracts a policy through advantage-weighted cloning. The corresponding private restricted-query proof is additional.
why: The logged-action restriction is part of the algorithm’s justification, not merely a data-format choice.
key_works: Ilya Kostrikov, Ashvin Nair, Sergey Levine (2022), [*Offline Reinforcement Learning with Implicit Q-Learning*, arXiv:2110.06169](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06169).

title: Full-vocabulary temperature-distillation gradient proofs
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Prove use of the committed teacher’s full temperature-scaled distribution, temperature-squared loss factor, hard-label mixture, and student update. Target 128K vocabulary and 2K-token sequences within 3× the cost of the required constituent forward/backward proofs, hiding teacher probabilities.
status: Classical distillation supplies the objective; zkDL supplies training-proof primitives. Their complete hidden-teacher integration at this scale remains a proposed target.
why: A top-k approximation can differ materially from the full distribution named in a training contract.
key_works: Geoffrey Hinton, Oriol Vinyals, Jeff Dean (2015), [*Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network*, arXiv:1503.02531](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531); Haochen Sun et al. (2023), [*zkDL*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16273).

title: On-policy distillation with proved sampling and stop-gradient boundaries
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Prove GKD’s fixed-data/student-generated mixture, teacher feedback on the exact sampled sequences, and stopped gradients through sampling and teacher parameters. Target a 7B student, 70B teacher, and \(10^5\) sequences below 10× the identical unproved recipe’s runtime.
status: GKD introduces student-generated distillation and alternative divergences. It does not supply this end-to-end ZK workload.
why: Different sequence sources or differentiation boundaries produce different learning algorithms.
key_works: Rishabh Agarwal et al. (2024), [*On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes*, arXiv:2306.13649](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.13649).

title: Cross-tokenizer sorted-probability distillation certificates
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Prove ULD’s padded, independently sorted probability vectors, tokenizer outputs, position pairing, tie rules, and student gradient. Target 32K/128K vocabularies over 2K paired positions with \(O(V\log V)\) auxiliary work and hidden token identities and ranks.
status: ULD provides a cross-tokenizer sorted-probability surrogate. Certifying that surrogate does not establish semantic equivalence of the vocabularies.
why: Tokenization and alignment choices otherwise sit outside the proved distillation loss.
key_works: Nicolas Boizard, Kevin El Haddad, Céline Hudelot, Pierre Colombo (2025 revision), [*Towards Cross-Tokenizer Distillation: the Universal Logit Distillation Loss for LLMs*, arXiv:2402.12030](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.12030v3).

title: Contrastive distillation with a private authenticated negative bank
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Bind positive teacher–student pairs, negative sampling, feature-bank versions, and projection-head state to the complete loss and gradient. Target a \(10^6\)-example bank and 16K negatives per update, with proof work proportional to accessed entries and hidden sample identities.
status: Contrastive Representation Distillation provides the representation-transfer objective. Private authenticated bank access and complete update proofs add separate obligations.
why: Forged or stale negatives can alter the objective while preserving valid arithmetic on supplied features.
key_works: Yonglong Tian, Dilip Krishnan, Phillip Isola (2020), [*Contrastive Representation Distillation*, arXiv:1910.10699](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10699).

title: IPO squared-margin stationary-point certificates
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Certify IPO’s squared log-ratio-margin objective and update direction on both sides of its finite target margin. Derive precision conditions perturbing the isolated scalar optimum by at most \(10^{-3}\), then prove private updates for batches of 1,024 preference pairs.
status: The ΨPO/IPO analysis supplies the squared-margin objective. A DPO score certificate does not establish IPO’s stationary point or gradient sign.
why: Numerical approximation can change the intended preference objective’s equilibrium.
key_works: Mohammad Gheshlaghi Azar et al. (2024), [*A General Theoretical Paradigm to Understand Learning from Human Preferences*, arXiv:2310.12036](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.12036).

title: KTO surrogate-reference and unpaired-label proofs
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Prove desirable/undesirable weighting, cyclically mismatched microbatches, clamped reference values, and stopped gradients through the reference. Target 4,096 unpaired examples with less than 10% overhead beyond likelihood/backward proofs, keeping labels and the reference private.
status: KTO’s September 2026 revision explicitly describes a biased KL surrogate and stopped-gradient reference. The certificate must name that surrogate rather than claim true KL.
why: A reference-estimation shortcut is part of the computation that needs to be disclosed and proved.
key_works: Kawin Ethayarajh, Winnie Xu, Niklas Muennighoff, Dan Jurafsky, Douwe Kiela (2024; revised 2026), [*KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization*, arXiv:2402.01306v5](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.01306v5).

title: ORPO odds-ratio numerics and joint-objective proofs
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Prove ORPO’s chosen-response likelihood and odds-ratio preference terms under one length-normalization convention and backward pass. For probabilities in \([2^{-24},1-2^{-24}]\), certify a gradient-error envelope and test \(10^6\) adversarial boundary cases.
status: ORPO defines a reference-free joint objective. Stable numerical certification and the complete private update remain proposed extensions.
why: Near-boundary logarithms can change gradients or invalidate naive lookup approximations.
key_works: Jiwoo Hong, Noah Lee, James Thorne (2024), [*ORPO: Monolithic Preference Optimization without Reference Model*, arXiv:2403.07691](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07691).

title: AOT distributional preference matching with private ranks
subfield: Distillation and alternative preference objectives
open: Prove complete empirical reward distributions, independent sorts, optimal-transport matching, and tie subgradients before an AOT update. Target 8,192 examples across 128 workers with \(O(B\log B)\) auxiliary work and hidden ranks.
status: AOT derives distributional alignment through one-dimensional optimal transport. An empirical proof does not establish population stochastic dominance.
why: Omitting observations or altering ranks changes the distributional objective.
key_works: Igor Melnyk et al. (2024), [*Distributional Preference Alignment of LLMs via Optimal Transport*, arXiv:2406.05882](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.05882).

title: Permutation-alignment optimality before private model merging
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Certify architecture-respecting hidden-unit permutations and optimality of each declared linear-assignment subproblem at width 16,384, targeting \(O(d^2)\) auxiliary work. Exact function preservation requires suitable fixed-point reductions; general floating-point implementations need a proved reordering-error bound.
status: Git Re-Basin supplies permutation-based alignment and merging. Global optimality over all layers, and exact GPU numerical equivalence, do not follow from that construction.
why: An algebraic symmetry may fail to preserve the deployed program’s numerical output.
key_works: Samuel K. Ainsworth, Jonathan Hayase, Siddhartha Srinivasa (2023), [*Git Re-Basin: Merging Models modulo Permutation Symmetries*, arXiv:2209.04836](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.04836).

title: TIES trimming, sign election, and survivor-denominator proofs
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Prove task-vector magnitude trimming, ties, sign election, averaging over the correct survivors, and the zero-survivor rule. Target merging 16 private 7B models within 3× the proof cost of weighted averaging over the same committed weights.
status: TIES-Merging establishes the three-stage merge algorithm. The matched private proof and comparative cost target remain additional.
why: A provider can manipulate contributors or denominators while reporting a plausible merged checkpoint.
key_works: Prateek Yadav et al. (2023), [*TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models*, arXiv:2306.01708](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01708).

title: Fisher-weighted merging with proved information estimators
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Specify predictive versus empirical Fisher information, then prove sample construction, squared-score accumulation, damping, weighted merging, and zero denominators. Target eight 7B models with less than 2× auxiliary proof cost beyond score-gradient proofs and merge arithmetic.
status: Fisher-weighted merging uses posterior-precision approximations. Arbitrary positive merge weights are not evidence of a correctly computed Fisher estimate.
why: The weighting estimator encodes the justification for the merge.
key_works: Michael Matena, Colin Raffel (2022), [*Merging Models with Fisher-Weighted Averaging*, arXiv:2111.09832](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.09832).

title: Synaptic-intelligence path-integral consolidation proofs
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Prove every prescribed gradient–parameter-change product, task-boundary normalization, damping, reset, and subsequent consolidation penalty. Target 1B parameters across 100 tasks with less than 5% extra proof cost and parameter-linear persistent state.
status: Synaptic Intelligence accumulates importance along the optimization path. Proving that accumulator does not guarantee absence of forgetting.
why: Final weights alone cannot establish how path-dependent importance values were obtained.
key_works: Friedemann Zenke, Ben Poole, Surya Ganguli (2017), [*Continual Learning Through Synaptic Intelligence*, arXiv:1703.04200](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04200).

title: GEM projection feasibility and optimality certificates
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Prove GEM’s gradient-projection QP using all required prior-task gradients, including feasibility, stationarity, complementary slackness, and a certified objective gap at most \(10^{-6}(1+\|g\|^2)\). Target 100 prior tasks and 100M parameters below 2× auxiliary cost over gradient proofs.
status: GEM supplies the constrained-update algorithm. First-order constraints do not guarantee exact non-increase of every nonlinear task loss.
why: Feasibility alone cannot certify that the intended projection was computed.
key_works: David Lopez-Paz, Marc’Aurelio Ranzato (2017), [*Gradient Episodic Memory for Continual Learning*, arXiv:1706.08840](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.08840).

title: Meta-training episode isolation and support/query dataflow
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: Prove that every episode within a MAML meta-batch starts from the prescribed initialization and episode-local optimizer/normalization state. Across \(10^6\) episodes, certify support/query disjointness and absence of query influence on inner updates, with less than 5% overhead beyond gradient proofs.
status: MAML establishes task-specific adaptation. Complete episode-state isolation is distinct from merely proving higher derivatives.
why: Hidden state carried between episodes can leak adaptation information and alter evaluation semantics.
key_works: Chelsea Finn, Pieter Abbeel, Sergey Levine (2017), [*Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning for Fast Adaptation of Deep Networks*, arXiv:1703.03400](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.03400).

title: Parameter-isolation proofs for prior-task behavior preservation
subfield: Model merging, continual learning, and episodic meta-training
open: For PackNet-style training, certify masks, frozen weights, task heads, and every mutable inference buffer used by prior tasks. Prove identical prior-task outputs under declared arithmetic for 100 tasks sharing a 7B network, with update work proportional to changed state.
status: PackNet uses pruning and parameter isolation. Frozen weights alone do not cover mutable normalization or other inference state.
why: A precise noninterference guarantee can support stronger claims than a sampled forgetting benchmark.
key_works: Arun Mallya, Svetlana Lazebnik (2018), [*PackNet: Adding Multiple Tasks to a Single Network by Iterative Pruning*, arXiv:1711.05769](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05769).

title: DoReMi proxy-to-training mixture certificates
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Prove reference/proxy losses, clipped excess losses, exponentiated reweighting, smoothing, and averaged domain weights, then bind main-model sampling to them. Target 64 domains, \(10^6\) proxy updates, and \(10^9\) main-training tokens below 5% auxiliary overhead.
status: DoReMi uses a proxy model to choose a larger model’s data mixture. Its two-stage private proof is a further target.
why: A certified training run can still use an unauthorized mixture unless mixture derivation is included.
key_works: Sang Michael Xie et al. (2023), [*DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining*, arXiv:2305.10429](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10429).

title: Self-paced curriculum inclusion and exclusion certificates
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Prove that each curriculum round includes exactly the examples selected by committed losses, latent assignments, and pace parameters, including excluded candidates. Target \(10^8\) records over 100 rounds with linear auxiliary work per round and hidden difficulties and selections.
status: Self-paced learning establishes loss-dependent admission. Certification at the proposed private scale adds a complete-selection obligation.
why: Proving selected examples alone permits undisclosed exclusion of difficult or inconvenient records.
key_works: M. P. Kumar, Benjamin Packer, Daphne Koller (2010), [*Self-Paced Learning for Latent Variable Models*](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2010/hash/e57c6b956a6521b28495f2886ca0977a-Abstract.html).

title: Private random-reshuffling epoch certificates
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Prove fresh prescribed random permutations of all committed record IDs, preserving multiplicity and binding update order. Target \(10^9\) records over 30 epochs with linear auxiliary work, less than 64 GB working memory, and explicit seed-generation and abort assumptions.
status: RandomShuffle theory distinguishes without-replacement epochs from IID sampling. A permutation-membership proof alone does not establish randomness.
why: Order manipulation can change training even when every record appears exactly once.
key_works: Jeff Haochen, Suvrit Sra (2019), [*Random Shuffling Beats SGD after Finite Epochs*](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/haochen19a.html).

title: Muon finite-iteration orthogonalization and shape-scaling proofs
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Prove Muon’s prescribed finite Newton–Schulz iterations, momentum, normalization, shape scaling, and decay. Target \(4{,}096\times16{,}384\) blocks with five iterations, less than 10× optimizer runtime, and at most two full auxiliary matrix buffers.
status: The 2025 scaling work specifies approximate finite iterations and shape-sensitive scaling. Substituting an exact polar factor would certify a different operation.
why: The approximation itself is part of the optimizer’s deployed semantics.
key_works: Jingyuan Liu et al. (2025), [*Muon is Scalable for LLM Training*, arXiv:2502.16982](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.16982v1).

title: Adafactor proving without dense second-moment expansion
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Prove the momentum-free Adafactor variant’s row/column accumulators, reconstructed scales, decay, clipping, and relative step size. For \(8{,}192^2\) blocks, retain \(O(m+n)\) persistent optimizer witness state and target auxiliary proof cost at most 2× proving the gradient tensor.
status: Adafactor reduces optimizer memory through factored second moments. Preserving that saving through the proof system is additional work.
why: A dense proof witness can negate the optimizer’s principal memory advantage.
key_works: Noam Shazeer, Mitchell Stern (2018), [*Adafactor: Adaptive Learning Rates with Sublinear Memory Cost*, arXiv:1804.04235](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.04235).

title: SAM perturbation, restore, and second-gradient binding
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Prove the first gradient, normalized perturbation, gradient at perturbed weights, restoration, and final SAM update under declared batch/randomness conventions. Target 1B parameters within 1.25× the proof cost of two ordinary gradient steps, including stopped gradients and normalization buffers.
status: SAM approximates a neighborhood min–max objective through a second pass. The certificate must cover that approximation rather than claim exact inner maximization.
why: A second gradient is meaningful only when bound to the correct perturbed state.
key_works: Pierre Foret, Ariel Kleiner, Hossein Mobahi, Behnam Neyshabur (2021), [*Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization*, arXiv:2010.01412](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01412).

title: MeZO paired perturbations and in-place restoration proofs
subfield: Data curricula and alternative optimizer state
open: Prove seeded directions, paired perturbations, finite-difference losses, restoration, and updates without reverse-mode activation storage. Target a 30B model on one 80 GB accelerator below 10× runtime, certifying loss cancellation and restoration roundoff or restoring committed originals exactly.
status: MeZO demonstrates forward-only fine-tuning, including a 30B single-80-GB-GPU workload without ZK. The corresponding proof-memory and numerical guarantees remain proposed.
why: Floating-point perturb-and-restore sequences need not return exactly to their starting weights.
key_works: Sadhika Malladi et al. (2023), [*Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes*, arXiv:2305.17333](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17333).

title: Dynamic-resolution image patch and merger conformance
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Prove decoded-pixel resizing, patch coordinates, window assignment, spatial merging, and vision-to-language token ordering. Cover 1,000 adversarial dimensions up to \(4{,}096^2\), require exact coordinate rules, and keep preprocessing/merging below 20% of vision-tower proving time.
status: Qwen2.5-VL specifies dynamic-resolution processing; ZKTorch provides composable ML proof blocks. Complete spatial-coverage certification is the extension.
why: An authentic vision tower can still receive the wrong crop, patch ordering, or image coverage.
key_works: Shuai Bai et al. (2025), [*Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report*, arXiv:2502.13923](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13923); Bing-Jyue Chen, Lilia Tang, Daniel Kang (2025), [*ZKTorch*, arXiv:2507.07031](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07031).

title: Learned visual resampler proofs with complete patch coverage
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Certify Q-Former or Perceiver-style resampling, binding learned queries, attention masks, projections, and ordering to committed visual features. Compress 4,096 visual tokens to 32–64 query tokens with at least 4× less peak witness memory than materializing all attention tensors.
status: BLIP-2 and Flamingo establish learned visual-compression architectures. They do not provide these ZK implementations.
why: Compression can hide omitted visual regions unless its complete input relation is proved.
key_works: Junnan Li et al. (2023), [*BLIP-2*, arXiv:2301.12597](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12597); Jean-Baptiste Alayrac et al. (2022), [*Flamingo*, arXiv:2204.14198](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198).

title: Waveform-to-log-Mel front-end certificates
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Prove channel mixing, resampling, padding, STFT, Mel filtering, log clipping, and normalization from committed PCM. For 60 seconds of 48-kHz stereo audio, target less than 10 seconds proving, a published spectrogram-error bound, and 10,000 framing-edge fixtures.
status: Whisper’s paper and implementation define the ordinary signal-processing path. Its complete proof must include preprocessing often left outside the neural circuit.
why: Proving the encoder alone does not bind its input features to the original recording.
key_works: Alec Radford et al. (2022), [*Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision*, arXiv:2212.04356](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356); OpenAI Whisper contributors, [*audio.py*](https://github.com/openai/whisper/blob/main/whisper/audio.py).

title: Variable-frame-rate audio-video time correspondence
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Certify frame selection, audio chunks, modality interleaving, and timestamp-to-position conversion, including dropped/repeated frames. On one-hour variable-frame-rate streams, require no undeclared timestamp reassignment and less than 10% alignment-proof overhead.
status: Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen2.5-Omni specify temporal and multimodal mechanisms. Proving chronology and routing is an additional obligation.
why: Correct per-modality inference can still combine observations from incompatible times.
key_works: Shuai Bai et al. (2025), [*Qwen2.5-VL Technical Report*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.13923); Jin Xu et al. (2025), [*Qwen2.5-Omni Technical Report*, arXiv:2503.20215](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20215).

title: Interleaved-image cross-attention routing proofs
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Prove the permitted image/video states for every text token, including sentinels, gated cross-attention, and encoder-state reuse. For 64 media items and 8,192 text positions, require exact masks and less than 5% routing overhead beyond attention arithmetic.
status: Flamingo makes interleaved visual/text sequences explicit. Generic attention proofs do not automatically bind cross-modal source selection.
why: A provider could attach valid features from the wrong image to a text position.
key_works: Jean-Baptiste Alayrac et al. (2022), [*Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning*, arXiv:2204.14198](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198).

title: Thinker–Talker branch and streaming-audio consistency
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Bind text generation, hidden representations passed to a speech branch, audio tokens, and waveform decoding into one state-transition proof. For ten minutes of output, target horizon-independent proof memory and first certified audio within two seconds after inference produces it.
status: Qwen2.5-Omni introduces Thinker–Talker and a streaming speech decoder. Text correctness alone does not certify the speech branch.
why: Users need assurance that spoken output follows the same approved computation as displayed text.
key_works: Jin Xu et al. (2025), [*Qwen2.5-Omni Technical Report*, arXiv:2503.20215](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20215).

title: Residual-quantization neural audio-codec proofs
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Prove residual-codebook selection, residual updates, bandwidth-dependent codebook count, and causal decoding state. For 60 seconds of 24-kHz audio, target proof generation within 60 seconds and final evidence below 1 MB, with exact fixed-point conformance.
status: EnCodec establishes streaming neural compression with quantized latent representations. A complete residual-codec proof remains a proposed extension.
why: Audio-token integrity is incomplete without binding tokens, codebooks, and delivered PCM.
key_works: Alexandre Défossez, Jade Copet, Gabriel Synnaeve, Yossi Adi (2022), [*High Fidelity Neural Audio Compression*, arXiv:2210.13438](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13438).

title: Long-form ASR seek, silence, and fallback integrity
subfield: Multimodal input, alignment, and output proofs
open: Prove overlapping windows, seek offsets, silence skipping, temperature fallbacks, and prior-text conditioning. For 30-minute recordings, require exact processed/skipped interval accounting with at most twice the witness memory needed for one window.
status: Whisper’s reference transcriber implements orchestration beyond the encoder-decoder network. Its faithful execution is distinct from semantic correctness of recognition.
why: A transcript can omit source intervals while all executed neural calls remain valid.
key_works: Alec Radford et al. (2022), [*Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.04356); OpenAI Whisper contributors, [*transcribe.py*](https://github.com/openai/whisper/blob/main/whisper/transcribe.py).

title: Denoiser parameterization and sampler-schedule conformance
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Prove prediction-parameterization conversion, schedule coefficients, timestep selection, preconditioning, and sampler boundaries. For a 50-step \(1{,}024^2\) latent-diffusion run, target scheduler proving below 10% of denoiser proving time and exact declared fixed-point semantics.
status: DDIM and EDM define ordinary sampling choices. ZK-WAGON proves selected generation-model layers, leaving complete iterative schedules outside that demonstrated scope.
why: The same denoiser checkpoint can implement different generators under different schedules.
key_works: Jiaming Song, Chenlin Meng, Stefano Ermon (2020), [*Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models*, arXiv:2010.02502](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502); Tero Karras et al. (2022), [*Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models*, arXiv:2206.00364](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00364); Aadarsh Anantha Ramakrishnan et al. (2025), [*ZK-WAGON*, arXiv:2510.01967](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01967).

title: High-dimensional discretized-Gaussian noise certificates
subfield: Diffusion, flow, and iterative-generation proofs
open: Certify \(2^{20}\) noise coordinates with unit standard deviation, grid \(2^{-16}\), support \([-12,12]\), and joint TV error at most \(2^{-40}\) against that finite law under uniform input bits. Bind counters and target at most 2× corresponding uniform-word expansion cost, accounting for practical PRGs through a separate computational argument.
status: Diffusion algorithms specify high-dimensional noise; the complete finite-law sampler guarantee is a proposed extension. A finite sampler must not be compared with a continuous law in TV distance.
why: Correct tensor arithmetic cannot protect the output distribution against chosen or correlated latent noise.
key_works: Jiaming Song et al. (2020), [*DDIM*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502); Tero Karras et al. (2022), [*Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.00364).

title: Adaptive high-order diffusion-solver transition proofs

title: Late-interaction MaxSim and residual-decoding proofs

why: Substituting embeddings or omitting a maximizing token can manipulate relevance scores.
key_works: Keshav Santhanam et al. (2022), [*ColBERTv2: Effective and Efficient Retrieval via Lightweight Late Interaction*, arXiv:2112.01488](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01488).

title: Complete-candidate cross-encoder reranking
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs
open: Bind a retrieved candidate multiset to every query–passage encoding, cross-encoder score, calibration, and final rank, proving each required candidate was scored exactly once. For 1,000 passages of 512 tokens, target less than 30 seconds on eight GPUs and below 5% bookkeeping overhead.

key_works: Rodrigo Nogueira, Kyunghyun Cho (2019), [*Passage Re-ranking with BERT*, arXiv:1901.04085](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04085); Bing-Jyue Chen et al. (2025), [*ZKTorch*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07031).

title: Shard-map-complete distributed retrieval merges

title: GraphRAG community and summary-dependency certificates

key_works: Darren Edge et al. (2024), [*From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization*, arXiv:2404.16130](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130).

title: Learned-sparse expansion and inverted-index pruning proofs
subfield: Structured, learned, and distributed retrieval proofs

title: Point-cloud sampling and set-abstraction certificates

title: Efficient uniqueness certificates for trained deep-equilibrium models
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures

key_works: Shaojie Bai, J. Zico Kolter, Vladlen Koltun (2019), [*Deep Equilibrium Models*, arXiv:1909.01377](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.01377).

title: NeRF hierarchical ray-sampling and compositing proofs
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures

key_works: Ben Mildenhall et al. (2020), [*NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis*, arXiv:2003.08934](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934).

title: Hypernetwork-generated weight integrity without repeated full commitments
subfield: Geometric, implicit, and dynamically parameterized architectures

For \(10^8\) edges and sampled subgraphs up to \(10^5\) vertices, target subgraph-proportional work, evidence below 1 MB, and hidden unvisited neighbors.

subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services

status: Wright’s 2022 disclosures document invalid-value acceptance in specialized proofs; those fixed defects provide context. Uniform machine-checked proof-decoding contracts remain the proposed target.

title: Cross-verifier differential acceptance corpus

title: Typed Fiat–Shamir transcript generation
subfield: Implementation security of numerical proof services
